1.text:
Did the Universe Have a Beginning?

In Deck 18 we zoomed out from single stars to whole galaxies. Now we take the biggest step of all: the entire universe and its history.

This deck asks one huge question: how do we know the universe had a beginning? It sounds like something no one could ever answer. But the universe left clues everywhere: in the colors of distant galaxies, in a faint glow that fills all of space, and in the recipe of the gas between the stars. Our job is to read them.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can explain how redshift shows the distance to galaxies is growing. I can use Hubble's law to link a galaxy's distance and speed. I can compare measurements of the Hubble constant. I can estimate the age of the universe from its expansion. I can model expanding space and explain why galaxies don't grow. I can explain why the observable universe is 46 billion ly in radius.

I can describe dark energy and the speeding-up expansion. I can use the CMB and the hydrogen-helium mix as Big Bang evidence. I can diagram energy cooling into protons, nuclei and atoms. I can explain how gravity built the first stars and galaxies. And I can explain why the CMB is studied with microwave telescopes, many in space. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.2, ES.1.3 and ES.1.1, plus some enrichment.

3.text:
Light from Galaxies Is Stretched

Remember spectral fingerprints from Deck 15? Every element makes its own pattern of lines. In the lab, hydrogen at rest always shows its lines in the same places.

Now look at a galaxy's spectrum. The same hydrogen pattern is there, but every line shifts toward red, toward longer wavelengths. That's called redshift: a galaxy's spectral lines shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. It means the galaxy is getting farther away.

On the slide, shorter wavelengths (blue) are on one side and longer wavelengths (red) are on the other. The galaxy's whole fingerprint has slid toward the red end.

Did you know? Vesto Slipher noticed in 1914 that most spiral galaxies are redshifted. Only a few close neighbors, like Andromeda, are moving toward us.

4.text:
The Farther, the Faster

Now for the pattern that changed everything. Hubble's law says the farther away a galaxy is, the faster its distance from us grows.

On the graph, each dot is one galaxy. Distance from us runs across the bottom, and how fast the distance grows runs up the side. The dots fall along a straight line. In math: v = H0 × d, where v is the speed, d is the distance, and H0 is the Hubble constant.

Speeds come from redshifts. Distances come from the distance ladder you built in Deck 18, using Cepheids and Type Ia supernovae.

Did you know? Georges Lemaître found this relationship in 1927, two years before Hubble published it. Today it's often called the Hubble-Lemaître law.

5.text:
How Fast Is Space Stretching?

The Hubble constant is about 70 km/s/Mpc. That means for every 1 Mpc (megaparsec, about 3.26 million light-years) farther away, a galaxy moves away about 70 km/s faster.

But there's a puzzle. Two careful measurements disagree. Planck 2018, using the CMB, measured 67.4. SH0ES 2022, using Cepheids plus Type Ia supernovae, measured 73. On the number line from 64 to 76, their error bars don't overlap.

This is called the Hubble tension. Scientists don't know yet whether it's a hidden measurement mistake or a sign of new physics. It's one of the hottest open questions in astronomy.

6.text:
Run the Expansion Backward

If galaxies are moving apart, they used to be closer together. Run the movie backward, and everything comes together at the Big Bang.

A quick estimate, called the Hubble time, is 1 ÷ H0. At 70 km/s/Mpc, that gives about 14 billion yrs. The careful Planck 2018 measurement gives 13.8 billion yrs, from the Big Bang to today.

There's a built-in cross-check. The universe has to be older than everything inside it. The oldest stars are about 13 billion yrs old. Earth is 4.54 billion yrs old. Both fit nicely inside 13.8 billion years.

7.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Use Hubble's law. Galaxy B is twice as far away as galaxy A. How fast does the distance to B grow?

Is it A) twice as fast as A, B) half as fast as A, C) the same speed as A, or D) B is getting closer? Look at the graph on Slide 4 and choose.

8.text:
The Raisin Bread Model

The expansion of space means space itself stretches, carrying galaxies farther apart. Galaxies aren't zooming through space. The space between them is growing.

Picture raisin bread rising in an oven. The raisins are galaxies, and the dough is space. In 1 hour, the loaf doubles: it's twice as big. A raisin that was 1 cm from our raisin is now 2 cm away. A raisin that was 3 cm away is now 6 cm away. That farther raisin's distance grew 3 times faster.

That's Hubble's law in a loaf of bread! And here's the key: every raisin sees all the others getting farther away. No raisin is the center.

9.text:
Galaxies Don't Get Bigger

If space is stretching, why don't galaxies stretch too? Because they're a bound system: a galaxy, group or cluster held together by its own gravity, so it does not expand.

Picture a balloon with flat stickers on it. The balloon skin is space, and the stickers are galaxies. As you blow it up, the distance between them grows, but the stickers stay the same size.

The same goes for you, your house, Earth and the Solar System. Forces holding them together easily win over the stretching of space.

Did you know? That's why Andromeda can move toward us even though distant galaxies are moving away. Our Local Group is held together by gravity.

10.text:
How Far Can We See?

Here's a brain-bender. The universe is 13.8 billion years old, so the oldest light we see has a travel time of 13.8 billion yrs. You might think the edge of what we can see is 13.8 billion ly away.

But space stretched while the light traveled. The source sent its light long ago, when it was much closer. Today, that source is about 46 billion ly away.

So the observable universe, the edge of what we can see today, has a radius of about 46 billion ly. That's more than three times the light's travel distance.

Did you know? Nothing travels through space faster than light. But space itself can stretch so that faraway galaxies move apart faster than light.

11.text:
The Expansion Is Speeding Up

Astronomers expected gravity to slow the expansion down. Early on, that's what happened: gravity slowed it. But later, dark energy sped it up. Today the universe is expanding faster and faster.

Dark energy is an unknown cause that makes the expansion speed up. It was discovered using Type Ia supernovae, which looked fainter, and so farther away, than expected.

And the cosmic budget is humbling. The universe is about 68% dark energy, about 27% dark matter, and only 5% atoms. Everything we can see, every star, planet and person, is just a tiny slice.

Did you know? The discovery of the speeding-up expansion earned the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

12.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Think about the raisins and the stickers. As the universe expands, what happens to the Milky Way itself?

Is it A) it stays the same size because gravity holds it together, B) it stretches bigger, like the dough, C) it moves toward the center of the universe, or D) it shrinks as space stretches? Look back at Slides 8 and 9 and choose.

13.text:
Not an Explosion

The name "Big Bang" makes people picture a bomb going off at one point in empty space. That's NOT what happened.

The Big Bang means the universe was hot and dense everywhere, then space began to stretch. Look at the grid on the right. Early on, every point was close together. Later, every point is farther from every other point. No point is the center.

So where did the Big Bang happen? Everywhere at once. There's no center and no edge for it to expand into.

Did you know? The name "Big Bang" started as a joking nickname from a scientist who didn't like the idea.

14.text:
The Big Bang's Afterglow

The cosmic microwave background, or CMB, is the leftover glow of the hot early universe, stretched into microwaves. It comes as faint microwaves from every direction in the sky.

Back then it was a 3,000 K glow, as hot as the surface of a cool star. But space has stretched since, and so did the light. Now its waves are about 1,100 times longer, in the microwave range.

It was found by accident in the 1960s, using the Holmdel Horn Antenna in New Jersey (photo from 1962). Two scientists, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, heard a hiss they couldn't get rid of. It was the afterglow of the Big Bang.

Did you know? Penzias and Wilson even cleaned pigeon droppings out of the antenna, thinking that might be the source of the noise.

15.text:
The Temperature of Space

The CMB has a temperature of 2.725 K, less than 3 degrees above absolute zero.

The graph shows COBE FIRAS data (Fixsen 1996) as squares, landing right on a perfect blackbody curve. That's the exact shape the Big Bang predicts for leftover heat. When this graph was first shown to astronomers, they gave it a standing ovation.

The Planck all-sky map shows tiny hot and cold spots, differences of only 1 part in 100,000. Those tiny spots matter a lot. They're the seeds that gravity later grew into galaxies.

16.text:
The Big Bang's Recipe

The Big Bang made more than light. In the first 3 to 4 minutes, it also cooked up the first elements. A proton plus a neutron made deuterium, and deuterium fused into helium-4 (⁴He).

The final recipe was about 75% H and 25% He. Hydrogen made up about 3/4 of the mass, helium about 1/4, and lithium just a trace.

Here's the test. Measured in old gas clouds, helium is 24.5%. The Big Bang's prediction is about 24.5% helium. They match!

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Think about how we observe the afterglow. Why do astronomers study the Big Bang's afterglow with microwave telescopes, often in space?

Is it A) its light was stretched into microwaves, and our air absorbs some of them, B) microwaves are the only light that travels through space, C) the afterglow is hot, like a microwave oven, or D) visible-light telescopes are too small? Use Slides 14 and 15 to decide.

18.text:
From Energy to Galaxies

As space stretches, the universe cools, so particles can stick together. Each drop in temperature let something new form.

In the first microseconds, there was only energy and quarks, hotter than anything. By 0.01 second, at about 100 billion K, there were protons and neutrons. At about 3 minutes, around 1 billion K, they fused into H and He nuclei. At about 380,000 yrs and about 3,000 K, the first atoms formed.

Then gravity took over. The first stars appeared after 100 million yrs, and galaxies under 300 million yrs. Today, the universe has cooled all the way down to 2.725 K.

19.text:
The Universe Turns Clear

For its first 380,000 yrs, the universe was a hot fog. Light bounced off loose electrons, so it couldn't travel far, like headlights in thick fog.

Then the universe cooled to about 3,000 K, when atoms formed. Electrons joined nuclei, making mostly hydrogen and helium atoms. With no loose electrons to bounce off, light could fly free. Suddenly the universe was clear.

That freed light is the CMB we see today. It's like a baby photo of the universe, taken at age 380,000 years.

20.text:
Gravity Lights the First Stars

The first stars were the first generation of stars, made of only hydrogen and helium, plus a trace of lithium. There were no heavier elements yet.

It started with a clump of H and He gas, and gravity pulled it in. Theory says the first stars were giants, 30 to 300 Suns of mass, shining by about 100 million yrs or later.

Big stars live fast and die young. Many exploded, making the first heavier elements. That started the recycling you learned about in Deck 18.

21.text:
Inflation: A Fast Start

Let's go back to the very first moment. Inflation is a theory that space may have grown by a trillion trillion times in less than a trillionth of a trillionth of a second.

Why do scientists think so? It explains why the CMB is so even: about 2.725 K in every direction. It explains why space is flat: WMAP measured it flat to within 0.4%. And it stretched tiny ripples that later grew into galaxies.

An honest caveat: inflation is strongly supported, not proven. No one has observed inflation directly.

22.text:
How Will It All End?

The Big Freeze is when space keeps expanding forever, stars burn out, and everything slowly goes cold and dark. Right now, it's the best bet, if dark energy stays the same.

Dark energy is about 68 to 70% of the universe. The expansion started speeding up about 9 billion yrs after the Big Bang. Other endings, a Big Rip or a Big Crunch, are possible but speculative.

In 2025, DESI hints dark energy may be changing, at 2.8 to 4.2 sigma. That's not yet a discovery. The answer depends on what dark energy is, and no one knows yet.

Did you know? In a Big Rip, dark energy would grow so strong it would tear apart galaxies, stars and even atoms. In a Big Crunch, everything would fall back together.

23.text:
Flowchart: Energy Cools into Atoms

Time to finish the story you started in Deck 18. This task matches standard ES.1.3. Draw five boxes: 1, hot energy. 2, quark soup. 3, protons and neutrons. 4, H and He nuclei. 5, atoms, with light set free.

Under each box, write the time and temperature from Slide 18. Draw a thermometer arrow from hot to cool under the row.

Tape it to the left of your Deck 18 gravity diagram, so the two together tell the whole story. Last line: why couldn't atoms form at 3 minutes?

24.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Put the history of the universe in order. Which list goes from first to last?

Is it A) quarks, protons, nuclei, atoms, B) atoms, nuclei, protons, quarks, C) protons, atoms, quarks, nuclei, or D) nuclei, quarks, atoms, protons? Use the timeline on Slide 18.

25.text:
Exit Ticket

You've traced the universe from its first instant to today. Show what you learned.

First, how do redshift and Hubble's law show that the universe is expanding? Second, name two other pieces of evidence for the Big Bang. Third, why is the Big Bang not an explosion from a center? Fourth, put these in order and say what let each one form: atoms, protons, helium nuclei, first stars.

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

26.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.2: describe the expanding universe, or Big Bang Theory, using evidence: the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law and the cosmic microwave background. ES.1.3: make a diagram, flowchart or explanation of how energy cooled into protons and early elements, and how those elements formed huge stars and galaxies. Explain how gravity pulls clouds of these elements together into stars and galaxies.

ES.1.1 is review: explain how we study space by observing every kind of light, using different telescopes and tools, like the microwave telescopes that study the CMB.
